newsitem.title: USA: Dow Jones results fail to placate critics.
newsitem.headline: Dow Jones results fail to placate critics.

text.p: Dow Jones & Co. Inc. Wednesday reported a nearly one-third drop in first quarter earnings, which were dragged down by a steep decline in profits at its financial information services unit.
The numbers did little to avert criticism expected to resurface at next Wednesday's shareholder meeting of a plan to plough $650 million into financial information services.
"Dow Jones Markets, formerly Telerate, performed worse than I thought it had" in the first quarter, said James Cramer, a shareholder critic of Dow Jones.
Dow Jones, which publishes The Wall Street Journal, reported net income of $25.4 million, or 27 cents a share, down from $37.6 million, or 39 cents per share, in the year-ago quarter.

The company predicted it would earn $1.20 to $1.40 per share for the year, in line with analysts' consensus expectation for $1.31 per share, according to the First Call service. Dow Jones earned $190 million, or $1.96 a share, in 1996.
"The good news is the publishing did very well, while information services were a little worse than expected," said analyst Ed Atorino of Oppenheimer & Co.
"Results overall met expectations," Atorino said.

Dow Jones has been criticised for giving shareholders miserable returns since its stock peaked a decade ago at $56 a share, before the 1987 stock market crash. On Wednesday, the stock fell $1 to $39.75 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange.

Some shareholders, including members of Dow Jones' controlling Bancroft family, have lashed out at the company's plans to spend $650 million catching up with its financial information service rivals, Reuters Holdings Plc and Bloomberg LP.

Cramer said he hoped three new independent Dow Jones directors -- American Express Chief Executive Officer Harvey Golub, Bankers Trust Co. CEO Frank Newman and Pfizer Inc. CEO William Steere -- would move the firm away from this idea.
"These are not guys who waste shareholder money," Cramer said. He hopes they will push for a sale of Dow Jones Markets.
"I reiterate this (a sale) is the right course of action, and management is on the wrong course of action," he said in an interview. Cramer bought a 1 percent stake in Dow Jones in January.
Dissident Dow Jones shareholder Michael Price, who bought a 4.7 percent stake the same month, said Wednesday the company should concentrate on what it does best, conventional business publishing.

Business publishing, including the Journal, Barrons weekly financial newspaper, television operations and Dow Jones Interactive Publishing group, posted operating income of $50.4 million, double 1996's first quarter.
Advertising linage at the Journal rose 21.7 percent in the quarter from a year ago.
But operating income in financial information services, which includes Dow Jones Markets and Dow Jones Newswires, tumbled 83.8 percent to $7.5 million.
"They admit Dow Jones Markets is struggling, but they said they were about on track with new developments," Atorino said.

Dow Jones on Tuesday announced a technology and marketing alliance with Microsoft Corp. to edge the firm into profitable areas like financial transaction systems and selling news to fund managers, the "buy-side" market.

Bloomberg has done well in this market, which is growing faster than the traditional "sell-side" market for information in big brokers' trading rooms, while Reuters has done well in transaction systems.

Price told the CNBC cable television station he expected Dow Jones to increase its dividend this year to around $1 per share from 96 cents per share for 1996, which he said will soak up 83 percent of expected earnings from 49 percent in 1996.

"(Chief Executive Officer) Peter Kann is paying a larger dividend in part because it helps him to justify his game plan to the family members," Price said. He added that a lower dividend would increase the share price.
